c.tagline: Where rugged mountains meet turquoise seas in Asia's youngest nation.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used in practice; agree the fare with the driver before departure.

emergency.medical: 110 (or Guido Valadares National Hospital emergency dept.)
emergency.note: Emergency numbers can be unreliable outside Dili; hotels/guesthouses can help contact help quickly.

avoid.reason: Petty crime; occasional martial-arts-group (gang) clashes/unrest — caution at night

hood_desc: The compact downtown core with government buildings, the central market and older colonial-era hotels; convenient for business travelers and short administrative visits.
A leafy, relatively affluent district with embassies, NGO offices and the Timor Plaza mall; suits longer-stay visitors and those wanting modern amenities and reliable wifi.
A quieter coastal stretch along the road toward the Cristo Rei statue, home to Dili's more resort-style properties; good for travelers wanting sea views, diving access and a calmer base.
Dili's popular white-sand beach neighborhood with waterfront cafes and a mix of budget-to-mid hotels; suits travelers who want to swim, watch sunsets and stay near the promenade.
A practical, low-key area near the airport with simple guesthouses; convenient for early departures or brief stopovers rather than for sightseeing.

water.note: Tap water is unsafe unless boiled or treated; use bottled water.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or conductor in small USD bills and coins; there is no rechargeable transit card. Mikrolets run informal numbered routes shown on the windshield and charge a flat fare regardless of distance.
transit.hours: Mikrolets and city buses generally run roughly 6am-8pm; there is little to no public transport after dark, so travelers rely on taxis or hotel transport at night.
transit.note: Public transport is informal with no fixed timetables; most visitors and long-term residents rely on taxis, hired drivers, or their own vehicle.

bus: Long-distance buses/minivans to Baucau, Same, Suai, Maliana and other districts depart from Dili's Taibesi and Becora terminals
ferry: Nakroma ferry to Atauro Island and Oecusse

transit.m: Fixed-fare taxi to city centre (~15 min)

tip.r: Tipping is not traditional in Timor-Leste but is increasingly appreciated at tourist-oriented restaurants and by drivers; rounding up is common.

food.name: Ikan sabuko
food.desc: Grilled mackerel marinated in tamarind, lime, garlic and chilli, wrapped in leaves and served with rice or cassava. Timor-Leste's signature fish dish.

places.name: Agora Food Studio
places.note: Social enterprise kitchen training young Timorese chefs; sabuko appears on the seasonal local menu.

places.name: Dilicious Timor
places.note: Built its reputation on Timorese produce and traditional fish preparations.

places.name: Beach Road grills
places.note: Evening open-air charcoal stalls; pick your fish and watch it grilled at sunset.

food.name: Batar daan
food.desc: Homely stew of corn, mung beans and pumpkin simmered until creamy. The everyday Timorese comfort dish and the classic partner to grilled fish.

places.name: Agora Food Studio
places.note: Serves batar daan as a side built from market vegetables bought that morning.

places.name: Dilicious Timor
places.note: Reliable place to try the corn-and-pumpkin stew alongside other village dishes.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Taibesi
places.note: Warung stalls around the market ladle batar daan over rice for a few dollars.

food.name: Tukir (bamboo-cooked meat)
food.desc: Goat, pork or buffalo chopped with onion, garlic and lemongrass, stuffed into green bamboo and roasted over embers until smoky and tender.

places.name: Agora Food Studio
places.note: Runs bamboo-cooked and ember-roasted dishes when the kitchen sources highland meat.

places.name: Ahoc Coffee & Restaurant
places.note: Local-cuisine menu covering the smoky roasted meat dishes Timorese eat at feasts.

places.name: Taibesi market food stalls
places.note: Weekend stalls sell bamboo and leaf-roasted meat brought in from the hills.

food.name: Grilled reef fish and seafood
food.desc: Snapper, tuna and squid straight off Dili's boats, grilled simply with lime, chilli and garlic. The city's best-loved way to eat dinner.

places.name: Tito's Restaurant
places.note: Long-running seafood address east of town, known for quality fish and traditional seasonings.

places.name: Beach Road grills
places.note: Dozens of open-air grills; the cheapest and liveliest seafood in the capital.

places.name: Dilicious Timor
places.note: Market-sourced fish cooked with Timorese herbs rather than imported sauces.

food.name: Katupa and Timorese rice plates
food.desc: Rice steamed in woven palm-leaf pouches, served with spiced meat, greens and sambal. Festival food that doubles as everyday street lunch.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Taibesi
places.note: Vendors sell katupa parcels and rice plates from early morning; the local staple market.

places.name: Ahoc Coffee & Restaurant
places.note: Sit-down version of the Timorese rice plate with several sides.

places.name: El Legendario
places.note: Authentic Timorese cooking with rice-and-stew combinations for lunch.

food.name: Tapai (fermented rice or cassava)
food.desc: Sweet-sour fermented rice or cassava with a faint alcoholic tang, eaten as a dessert or snack and often wrapped in banana leaf.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Taibesi
places.note: Leaf-wrapped tapai parcels sold by market women alongside cassava and corn snacks.

places.name: Mercado Lita
places.note: Neighbourhood market where fermented rice snacks turn up on the sweets tables.

places.name: Agora Food Studio
places.note: Uses traditional ferments in desserts and pairs them with local fruit.

food.name: Timor arabica coffee
food.desc: Organic highland arabica from Ermera, Letefoho and Maubisse, usually roasted dark. Timor-Leste's proudest export, drunk black and strong.

places.name: Letefoho Specialty Coffee Roaster
places.note: Roasts and brews single-origin beans from its own Letefoho estate; Dili's coffee benchmark.

places.name: Ahoc Coffee & Restaurant
places.note: Local roaster-cafe pairing Timorese coffee with pastries and breakfast.

places.name: Agora Food Studio
places.note: Serves Timorese single origins alongside its local-produce menu.

food.name: Tua mutin (palm wine)
food.desc: Milky sap tapped from lontar palms, drunk fresh and lightly fizzy; distilled further it becomes the fiery tua sabu. Village drink, sold roadside.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Taibesi
places.note: Palm sap arrives from the districts in jerrycans and bottles most mornings.

places.name: Roadside stalls, Comoro to Tibar
places.note: Classic tapping country on the coast road; bamboo tubes of fresh tua sold at the gate.

places.name: Castaway Bar
places.note: Beachfront bar where visitors can ask for local palm spirit alongside the usual drinks.

landmarks: Cristo Rei of Dili
A towering 27-meter bronze-and-copper statue of Christ atop a globe, perched on a hilltop peninsula with sweeping views over the Timor Sea and coastline.
Palácio do Governo (Government Palace)
The elegant Portuguese colonial-era government palace facing Dili's waterfront, a photogenic symbol of the nation's administrative heart and history.
Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception (Dili Cathedral)
Southeast Asia's largest Catholic cathedral, a striking white landmark reflecting Timor-Leste's deep Catholic heritage forged under Portuguese rule.
Areia Branca (White Sand Beach)
A relaxed palm-fringed beach just east of downtown Dili, popular with locals and visitors for sunset swims, seafood stalls, and coastal photography.
Motael Church
Dili's oldest church, a charming whitewashed building facing the harbor, cherished as a peaceful spiritual landmark tied to the city's colonial past.
Santa Cruz Cemetery
A somber, historically significant cemetery, site of the 1991 massacre, now a poignant pilgrimage stop for understanding Timor-Leste's independence struggle.
Timor Plaza
Dili's modern shopping, hotel, and entertainment complex, a striking contemporary contrast to the city's colonial architecture and a hub for visitors.
Resistance Museum (Arquivo & Museu da Resistência Timorense)
A moving museum documenting Timor-Leste's decades-long fight for independence through photographs, artifacts, and personal testimonies of resilience.
National Parliament Building
The bright yellow seat of Timor-Leste's legislature, a distinctive and photogenic architectural landmark symbolizing the young nation's democracy.
Tais Market
A vibrant market selling traditional handwoven tais textiles, offering visitors a colorful, hands-on introduction to Timorese craft and culture.

train.note: Timor-Leste has no railway at all. Overland travel is by road (minibus/bus) or by domestic ferry; long-distance visitors usually fly into Dili's Presidente Nicolau Lobato airport.

intl.to: Kupang, West Timor (Indonesia) - ~12 hr via the Batugade/Motaain border
intl.op: Timor Tour & Travel / Paradise Travel — book by phone a day ahead, no website

bus.note: A daily cross-border minibus links Dili with Kupang in Indonesian West Timor (about 12 hours via the Batugade/Motaain border), run by small operators such as Timor Tour & Travel and Paradise Travel; there is no website, so book by phone a day ahead and carry your passport plus an Indonesian visa. No other international bus routes exist.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international passenger ferry from Dili. Domestically, the government-run Berlin Nakroma ferry and fast boats connect Dili with Atauro Island and the Oecusse enclave from Dili's waterfront ferry terminal.

half.name: Atambua
half.blurb: Border town on Timor island known as a trading crossroads in eastern Indonesia.

half.name: Suai
half.blurb: Coastal town in southern Timor-Leste known for its coffee-growing region and coastline.
